one_liner: KDDI's reference C code for Rocca-S, a 256-bit-key AES-round AEAD; ~1.9-2.9x OpenSSL AES-128-GCM encryption throughput.
what_it_does: This is the designers' reference implementation of Rocca-S (ESORICS 2023; IETF individual draft draft-nakano-rocca-s), an AEAD for beyond-5G/6G links with a 256-bit key, a 128-bit nonce and a 256-bit tag. The API is five C calls on a caller-owned context: rocca_init, rocca_add_ad, rocca_encrypt or rocca_decrypt, and rocca_tag, which only outputs the tag. There is no verify call and no EVP-style interface, and the ciphertexts are not AES-GCM compatible. The entry also covers jedisct1's ports, zig-rocca-s (Zig) and the `rocca` crate (repo rust-rocca-s, Rust). Both offer one-shot encrypt/decrypt calls with a built-in constant-time tag check.
how_it_is_fast: Rocca-S is an AEGIS-style stream AEAD built from bare AES rounds. The state is seven 128-bit words. Each 32-byte block is absorbed through six independent AESENC rounds, with state words or message halves as round keys, plus one XOR; the keystream costs two more rounds. That is 8 AES rounds per 32 bytes, against AES-128-GCM's 10 rounds per 16 bytes plus a GHASH multiply, and there is no key schedule. The rounds in each step are independent, so they pipeline on AES-NI or ARM AESE/AESMC units, and the macros keep the whole state in __m128i registers for an entire call. Decryption is slower because each plaintext block is only known after its keystream AES round, which adds a round of latency to the state-update chain.
when_to_use: You need Rocca-S itself, for example to interoperate with KDDI's beyond-5G/6G experiments or with their Rocca-S forks of libsodium and msquic (yt-nakano/Rocca-S-libsodium, yt-nakano/Rocca-S-msquic).
Encrypt-heavy bulk AEAD on x86-64 with AES-NI, where you control both ends. At 64 KB on Zen 4 it encrypts at 174.6 Gbps vs 92.7 Gbps for OpenSSL AES-128-GCM.
Messages of several KB and up. The Zig port's M4 table climbs from 4.67 Gbps at 64 B to 70 Gbps at 1 KB and 190 Gbps at 64 KB.
Rust or Zig code that wants Rocca-S with a safe API: the `rocca` crate (no_std, in-place variants) or zig-rocca-s, which check the tag in constant time and overwrite the plaintext on failure.
As a known-answer reference: the gtest suite checks the draft's test vectors, which is useful for validating other implementations.
when_not_to_use: Decrypt-heavy or symmetric traffic. At 64 KB, decryption runs at 140.4 Gbps on M5 Max (1.48x slower than encryption), and on Zen 4 its 92.3 Gbps merely ties OpenSSL AES-128-GCM's 92.9 Gbps. AEGIS-128x2 decrypts at 213.1 Gbps on the same M5.
Anything that needs a standard, FIPS or interop. The spec is an individual draft that CFRG never adopted, it expired on 2026-08-01, and its IANA codepoint is still 'TBD'.

Settings that need key commitment, such as multi-key or password-derived decryption, partitioning-oracle exposure or message franking. ePrint 2024/901 gives practical committing attacks with a test vector. Nonce reuse leaks the XOR of the plaintexts (draft section 3.3).

ARM or other non-AES-NI targets with yt-nakano's code. There is no ARM crypto backend: the fallback is a T-table AES, which is slow and leaks through cache timing. The Rust crate likewise uses softaes's 'unprotected' tables on anything except x86 built with +aes, and that includes aarch64.
If you need a maintained C library. The reference has 2 stars, no CI and no releases, and its CMake test build hard-codes GCC 12 x86_64-linux-gnu include paths.

integration.form: source-drop (rocca-s_ref.c + rocca-s.h). The CMakeLists builds a shared lib with -O3 -march=native. The ports ship as a Rust crate (`rocca`) and a Zig package.
integration.dependencies: The library needs only libc, plus <immintrin.h> when __AES__ is defined. The bundled CMake unconditionally adds the test directory, which does find_package(GTest REQUIRED) and find_package(absl REQUIRED), so the stock build needs GoogleTest and Abseil. The Rust crate needs softaes on non-AES-NI targets.
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (the benchmark copy builds with -std=c99), CMake 3.14+, C++ for the tests. The Zig port tracks Zig 0.16/master (its benchmark uses std.Io). The Rust crate is edition 2018.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI, chosen at compile time via __AES__ (needs -maes or -march=native). Everything else, including aarch64, gets a portable T-table fallback. The ARM-crypto (vaeseq/vaesmcq) backend behind the M5 numbers exists only in the hiae-aead/benchmarks copy. The Zig port uses std.crypto.core.aes.Block. The Rust crate gets AES-NI only with RUSTFLAGS target-feature=+aes and falls back to soft AES elsewhere.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. There is no global state and rocca_context is caller-owned and per-message, so separate contexts on separate threads are independent.

gotchas: rocca_decrypt writes plaintext without authenticating it. You must call rocca_tag, compare the 32-byte tag in constant time yourself, and erase the output on mismatch, as draft section 3.4 recommends. The context holds the raw key and is never wiped. The Zig and Rust ports do the comparison and fill the output with 0xaa on failure.

It is not a real streaming API. Each rocca_add_ad/rocca_encrypt/rocca_decrypt call zero-pads its trailing partial block and advances the state, so every call except the last must be a multiple of 32 bytes, and all AD must come before the first encrypt/decrypt. Nothing enforces either rule.

The backend is fixed at compile time. A generic x86-64 build without -maes silently falls back to the table-based AES. The Rust README likewise says to export RUSTFLAGS="-Ctarget-feature=+aes,+sse4.1" for decent x86 code.

Only 256-bit keys and 16-byte nonces are implemented. Draft-06 also allows 12-16-byte nonces and 128/192-bit keys with a key-length-dependent S[6], added after ePrint 2024/901. Zero-padding a short key into this code reproduces the older expansion that has equivalent keys, so derive 256 bits with a KDF instead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same hiae-aead harness, libhiae's HiAE beats Rocca-S at both encryption and decryption (266.7/171.4 Gbps on M5, 268.4/139.1 on Zen 4), and libaegis's AEGIS-128x2 ties it on encryption and decrypts 1.5x faster (211.8/213.1 on M5), and AEGIS also has a separate constant-time bitsliced implementation (aegis-bitsliced). Pick Rocca-S only when the protocol requires Rocca-S; the original Rocca entry is its predecessor, which has published key-recovery and forgery attacks on v2-v4.
verified_claims_summary: jedisct1's hiae-aead/benchmarks harness ran a reformatted copy of this reference, with an added ARM-crypto backend, against OpenSSL EVP AES-128-GCM at 64 KB with 48 B of AD and the tag included. On an M5 Max (Apple clang 21.0.0, OpenSSL 3.6.4, -O3 -mcpu=native, median of three passes) it reached 208.1/140.4 Gbps encrypt/decrypt vs 70.8/70.2 (~2.9x/2.0x), with keystream 228.8 vs AES-128-CTR 159.6. On a Ryzen 7 7700 locked at 3.8 GHz (clang 21.1.8, OpenSSL 3.5.5, -O3 -march=native) it reached 174.6/92.3 vs 92.7/92.9, so ~1.9x on encryption and parity on decryption. Note that this pits 256-bit-key Rocca-S against AES-128, not AES-256-GCM.
status_note: The reference is stale: its last commit (2025-03-19) was a one-file update after the 2023 upload, and it has 2 stars and no issues. It is MIT-licensed and a single ~22 KB C file, so vendoring is easy. The maintained routes are jedisct1's MIT Zig port (21 stars, updated for Zig 0.16 in 2026) and the Rust crate `rocca` 0.3.2 (released 2026-09-25, ~7.7k downloads; Cargo.toml says MIT but the repo has no LICENSE file). yt-nakano's separate Rocca-SX repo (parallel SX2/SX4 variants, January 2026, no README) is a different, unspecified cipher.
